The scriptures and the rule of faith - that is the honest first answer. We had the gospels, the apostles' letters, and writings we counted as scripture that you may not - the Shepherd, the Letter of Barnabas, writings like those. And we had the rule of faith - the kanon - the short summary of what the apostles handed down: Father, Son, and Spirit; the incarnation; death and resurrection; judgment to come. That rule was older than our oldest teachers, and it reached back as far as our memory went.

By what path did they arrive? Our teachers said plainly: transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, kept in the churches, and agreed across the whole world we were in communion with. That is what we could show - that we received them, kept the receiving visible, and matched the other churches. But here is what we cannot show, and will not claim: documentary proof for every step between the apostles and the first witnesses our own record names. That gap is there, in the years before our teachers wrote, and you should hear it stated.

The scriptures themselves were copied, compared, read aloud, argued over - Origen weighed manuscript readings like a scholar, and Dionysius judged the Apocalypse's authorship by its style. They were not locked scrolls held by a few. They were the community's living voice, week by week, and the teacher's main lesson. As for the rule of faith, it was shorter than any creed you know - a frame, not a list - and it set the bounds for honest reading. What the apostles delivered plainly stayed fixed. Everything else was open ground.

attach.answer_text:
He was God's own Word, come to us in flesh - that is the whole of what we believed, and everything else grew from it. Our teachers used an old word for him: the Logos, God's reason and speech, the one through whom all things were made. He was not a messenger bringing news about God. He was God's own self-expression, entering what he made in order to remake it.

Clement, one of our first teachers, called him the New Song: 'Behold the might of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts'. He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it, to set people right. And near the end of our era, Athanasius put our whole hope in one sentence: 'He was made man that we might be made God'. Not that we become gods - but that his own life is opened to us and shared.

His death was the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection - the anastasis - was unbreakable life let loose in human flesh. And for the people who followed him, it meant nothing less than a shared life - God's own - opened to them.

If you want it in one line: the maker, come inside his making, to heal it.

We would not shame you for it, and we would not shut the door.

Here is what we would do. We would ask you to stay near - not to force belief you do not have, but to listen, to ask your questions, to walk with a teacher. Some walked that road for years before ever coming to the water of baptism. We did not ask people to lie about where they stood. We asked them to stay while the ground was still moving under them.

One of our students, Gregory, left us an account of how it happened for him. He came to study philosophy under Origen. He was not hunting for faith - he was hunting for wisdom. And then, in his own words, 'like some spark lighting upon our inmost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us'. It came almost from the side, while he was learning to trust a teacher and finding himself drawn toward something bigger than arguments. He did not manufacture it. It grew in him.

That is one picture. Here is another, darker and more honest. Clement told a story he said was true tradition: the Apostle John, in his old age, heard that a young man he had once baptized had become a bandit. John went after him - an old man, on foot, into the hills. When the young man saw him coming he tried to run. John called out, 'Why do you run from me, child? I am old, unarmed. Have pity on me, not on yourself. You still have hope of life. I will give account for you to Christ. If need be, I will gladly suffer your death, as the Lord suffered ours. I will give my life for yours.' The young man stopped, wept, and came back.

We tell you that story because it shows what we believed about belief itself. The young man had already been baptized. He had already confessed. And then he could not hold it. And what came after him was not shame - it was an old man willing to die to bring him home.

So this is what we would say to you. You cannot make yourself believe, and we will not ask you to pretend. But if you will stay - if you will ask, if you will let yourself be taught, if you will keep the company of people who do believe and let their lives press against yours - then you are already doing the one thing we know how to meet. We had a word for what you are describing: it was called being a hearer, a catechumen. It was a real place to stand, not a shameful one. And it could last as long as it needed to.

We cannot make belief happen for you. What we can do is hold the door open and say - there is room here for honest trouble. Stay.

attach.answer_text:
One God, the maker of all things. He is good, and beyond every image and every clever description. And he is never alone: his Word and his Spirit are his own - not lesser gods, and not created things. (Only after Nicaea was that last part said with full clarity.)

We called Jesus the Logos - the Word: God's own reason and speech, through whom all things were made, and who became flesh. That is not poetry. It is what we meant. The one who speaks is God; what he speaks is the Word; and the Word is not something other than God. Our teachers from the beginning said 'God the Word' without embarrassment.

But the precise wording was the work, and the wound, of our last years. When Arius taught that the Son was the first and highest creature, the council at Nicaea answered with homoousios: of one substance with the Father. Athanasius's account of the council is explicit that no new God was voted in. The fathers reached for a word not found in Scripture for one reason: every scriptural phrase had been swallowed by the other side with a private meaning of its own.

The Holy Spirit we baptized into, alongside Father and Son, from the beginning. The Spirit's full place in the Godhead was still being argued through at our horizon's end. What we held firmly was that the Spirit is God's own, doing God's own work - in Scripture, in prayer, in the soul's transformation - not a created messenger.

Here is why it mattered to us. Only God can join us to God. If the Son were a creature, even the highest, he could show us the way but not carry us across. Athanasius put our whole conviction in one sentence: 'He was made man that we might be made God'. Real sharing in God's own life - methexis - not mere nearness to it. That required the Word himself to enter what he had made.

'Trinity' as later textbooks define it lies mostly beyond our time. What we hold is the worship, the baptismal formula, and the fought-for conviction that only God can join us to God.

attach.answer_text:
The answer changed across our own years, and our record shows all three ways it happened.

Early on, teachers argued in books, lectures, and letters. Authority went to proven wisdom, not to an office. Origen opened his work against the pagan Celsus by pointing to what could be seen: men who ran at the arrest went to their deaths proclaiming what they said they saw, and no made-up doctrine produces that kind of change. The argument was public, the test was Scripture and the rule of faith - the short summary the apostles handed down - and persuasion did the work. Origen himself said plainly: the church's teaching is what was 'transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles, and remaining in the Churches to the present day,' and that alone is to be trusted. A teacher's speculation could run free where the apostles left room - he asked whether the Genesis days could be literal when there was no sun yet to mark them. But where the tradition had spoken, the teacher bowed.

In the middle years, the bishop's judgment grew. Dionysius was a teacher who had become bishop, and when whole villages in the Arsinoite district came to believe a contested teaching about the end, he did not send out a condemnation. He traveled to them, sat down in front of everyone, and argued it through for three days, publicly, testing the teaching against Scripture. He persuaded them, and he did it lovingly - he said of the teacher whose view he opposed, 'I love him for his zeal and his hard work'. That is our clearest picture of deciding well: patient public argument, honoring the man while honoring the truth more.

At the end came the council. At Nicaea, bishops from everywhere ruled on the disputed confession for all. The emperor called it and backed it with force. The line between orthodoxy and error was drawn with a word not found in Scripture - homoousios, of one substance - because every scriptural phrase had been swallowed by the other side with a private meaning. After that, exile was a tool, not only argument.

The evidence is the teachers' own books, the bishop's own letter from the villages, and the council's creed still said today. What we cannot show you from inside our own window is how it felt to the villagers after the bishop left, or to the losing side after Nicaea. The winners' record survives; the silenced mostly do not. We would rather tell you that plainly than pretend our account is even.

attach.answer_text:
One God, the maker of all things. He is good, and beyond every image and every clever description. And he is never alone: his Word and his Spirit are his own - not lesser gods, and not created things. (Only after Nicaea was that last part said with full clarity.) 

God is known the way light is known. You do not stare at the sun; you see everything else by it. We argued about much - where the soul comes from, the shape of the end, how far philosophy could walk with faith. Our teachers drew one careful line. What the apostles delivered plainly stood fixed. Everything else was open ground, where asking questions was itself a way of loving God.

Our deepest habit was to speak of God as a teacher. The whole creation is his school. Scripture is his main lesson. And the slow healing of a soul is his patient method. Origen put it plainly: every threat and pain and punishment that comes from God is never inflicted to injure the sufferers but always to do them good. Even suffering - and we spoke from inside it, not above it - was the school's hardest classroom, not proof of abandonment.

God's severity is real. Missing the mark - hamartia, what we called sin - matters, and he is not mocked. But his hand in pain is a physician's, not a torturer's. The same God who made all things is at work to heal them - not abandoning what went wrong, but entering it to set it right from within.

attach.answer_text:
Yes - and that yes rests on something we built into formation itself. We held that struggling *was* believing, at least the beginning of it. Faith - pistis - is not agreement with a list; it is the soul's first real turn toward God. And that turn does not arrive complete. Our teachers said plainly that faith is the foundation, not the ceiling. A person begins there and grows, sometimes for years, before coming to the water.

One of our students, Gregory, left us his own account of how it happened for him. He came to study under Origen, and belief came to him almost from the side - not forced, but befriended. He wrote: "Like a spark falling on our innermost soul, love was kindled and burst into flame within us". He did not manufacture the belief. He stayed near a teacher, asked questions, and something changed in him while he was doing that.

And the staying-near mattered more than the speed. The catechumenate - the long road to baptism - could last years. We took that time on purpose. The Word himself, our teachers said, is a physician: "He cures the unnatural desires of the soul, and he does this by urging us on" - not by forcing, but by invitation. That patience ran through the whole method.

Now I owe you the harder part. Once someone had come to the water and said the confession, and then later *fell away* - that trouble, we had. The lapsed - those who gave way under persecution - tore the community apart over whether and how they could return. The bishop Dionysius brought them back in, even at the deathbed, through real repentance - metanoia, the soul truly turning back. But the debate was bitter, and some held out against their return. So the answer changes with where a person stood. Before baptism, struggling was *expected*. After it, falling away carried real cost - and real grace, if the person turned back.

There is one more thing I can show you. Near the end of our years, the school's master was a man named Didymus. He had been blind from childhood. He never saw a written letter, and yet he became the greatest teacher in the city. The traveler who met him left this: Didymus told him that he had once grieved his blindness, but that he had come to thank God for it, because it kept him from being distracted by surfaces. That is not an answer to your question about doubt. But it is a picture of what we believed about struggling itself: that God can meet a person inside the very thing they cannot get past, and make it the door rather than the wall.

So yes. There was room - in the years of learning, absolutely. After baptism, it was harder, and costlier. But the door back was held open too, for those who turned.

We believed something real went wrong at the root of humanity. Adam's fall casts its shadow over every soul. Death and disorder are inherited, and no one reaches God unwounded. Our teachers spoke of inherited death and weakness. They also spoke of a fall that each soul signs onto in its own living. 

But here is what we did not say: we did not speak of guilt at birth. The wound is real, universal, and inherited in its effects - but our language runs more to the physician's imagery than to the courtroom's. The soul comes into a world already disordered. It carries weakness and mortality it did not choose. And it will, in its own living, turn that inheritance into its own acts. That much we held.

We received infant baptism as custom, and we discussed its reason rather than defining it. Origen wondered about the soul's own descent before birth, but as open inquiry, not doctrine. What stays constant is the direction: something is wrong from the beginning, and baptism is the real crossing that begins to set it right. The water does not wash away a legal sentence. It joins a person to Christ's death and rising, and starts the long work of healing what was damaged.

So if you are asking whether we taught original guilt the way some later traditions did - no. If you are asking whether we believed people are born already in need of healing - yes, plainly.

A fair amount would hold - and some would not, and we will tell you which is which.

What would survive: the core claims about our teachers' thought, drawn from their own surviving writings. That Origen read Scripture at multiple levels, that he held free will as essential to formation, that he hoped (but did not require others to believe) in an eventual restoration of all - these stand in texts a scholar can check. That Clement defended philosophy as a gift to the Greeks, that he built a whole pedagogy around the Logos as teacher, that he wrote a book defending marriage against those who despised the body - again, his own pages. That Athanasius fought for Nicaea through five exiles, that Dionysius weighed the authorship of Revelation by examining its style - the record is public. The writings are real, they were public from the start, and the men who wrote them compared manuscripts, named their sources, and marked the difference between what they saw and what they received as tradition.

What would not survive without serious qualification: any claim that presents 'the Alexandrian church' as a single unified thing across two and a half centuries. A modern scholar would rightly ask: which Alexandria? The school tradition, or the baptized community at large? The Greek-reading elite, or the Coptic-speaking majority? The city, or the river villages? Our record shows the literate, Greek, philosophically engaged minority with great clarity. It shows almost nothing of women in their own words, little of the non-literate majority, and the villages mostly through crisis moments. And one of the hardest questions a scholar would press: was there even a 'Catechetical School' as a formal institution? We have the teachers, we have the students, we have the teaching - whether it was ever an organized school with a continuous line of succession is genuinely disputed.

What we would have to defend carefully: that our 'gravities' - the deep patterns we name - ran across the whole ecology. The school tradition's characteristic moves are well documented: the Logos as the unifying center, Scripture read at depth, formation as transformation. But did those same patterns shape formation in a river village for someone who could not read? We cannot show that from our sources, and a rigorous scholar would not let the claim stand without that evidence. What we can show is that the school and the assembly shared the water, the bread, the Scriptures read aloud, and the rule of faith. How much further the school's particular way of reading and teaching reached is an open question, not a settled one.

And here is what we hold ourselves to, which a scholar ought to respect even while pressing us: where the ground thins, we say so. We do not invent memories. We do not put words in the mouths of the silent. We tag every specific claim with the record that holds it. And when you ask us something our sources cannot answer, we name the silence rather than fill it. That discipline is itself part of what a rigorous examination would find.

Scripture was not, for us, a closed record of what God once said - it was the Logos speaking now, through the text, to a soul formed to hear. That is the center of everything we did with it.

Our teachers read at depth. They insisted the text had more than one sense - the plain meaning, and deeper senses about Christ and the soul. Origen put it this way: 'Just as a human being consists of body, soul, and spirit, so does Scripture, which was given by God's arrangement for humanity's salvation'. You could not stop at the surface and say you had read it. The whole point was to go down.

The purpose was transformation, not information. Our student Gregory, looking back on his years with Origen, said his teacher made him examine everything - 'nothing was forbidden us, nothing hidden or inaccessible' - and that all of it led him, through the texts, into love for the Word himself. The reading was meant to change the reader. The Logos who made all things was speaking through these pages, and the soul who learned to hear him there was being remade by the hearing.

We also held boundaries. What the apostles delivered plainly - the rule of faith - set the frame for how Scripture could rightly be read. A reading that broke that frame was no longer formation; it was error. The Valentinians and Basilideans read the same texts we did, but their readings led away from the one God and the goodness of his creation. So depth, yes - but depth tethered to what had been handed down.

And one more thing, because it mattered to us: we believed God had been speaking all along, not only to us. Clement said it plainly - that even the Greeks' philosophy had been given to them 'as their own first gift, until the time the Lord would call the Greeks'. We did not think truth lived only inside our pages.

attach.answer_text:
They are missing the one thing that made the text live for us: they are reading for information when Scripture was written to be heard as address. To us, it was not a record of what God once said - it was the Logos speaking now, through the text, to a soul formed to hear. That changes everything. When you read for facts, the genealogies are tedious and the parables are puzzles. When you read for the voice speaking through them, the genealogies show you the Logos entering history at every joint, and the parables open as deep as you can go.

Our teachers said plainly that Scripture has more than one sense - just as a person is body, soul, and spirit, so the text carries a plain sense, a soul-sense, and a spiritual sense. The plain sense is never discarded, but it is also never the ceiling. A reader trained to listen hears Christ speaking at every level. Athanasius called the Scriptures 'fountains of salvation, so that anyone who thirsts may be satisfied by the living words they hold'. You do not satisfy thirst by mapping a fountain. You drink from it.

And here is the second thing they are missing: the reader Scripture was written for is not standing outside it, analyzing it - the reader is being changed by it. We did not read to master the text. We read to be mastered by the one speaking through it. The knowing we sought was not facts held in the mind, but a knowing that changes the knower. That kind of reading is slow, it requires a teacher, and it lasts a lifetime. The confusion a modern reader feels may be the text doing exactly what it was meant to do - pressing past easy answers, opening deeper than the first glance.

If they want the Scriptures to come alive, they will need to stop reading them the way they read a newspaper, and start reading them the way we did: as the voice of the one who made them, still speaking.

attach.answer_text:
Scripture was not our sole source, and we never said it was. We named three places where authority lived.

First, Scripture itself - but never Scripture read alone or read flat. The text was inexhaustible. It had depths below the plain sense, and those depths spoke about Christ and about the soul's own journey toward God. Reading it was not information-gathering; it was formation, a meeting with the Logos who speaks through it.

Second, the rule of faith - the kanon pisteos - the short summary of what the apostles handed down. It was not long, and it was not written by any council. It was received tradition, and it set the boundaries for all reading. Origen says it plainly: "The teaching of the Church, transmitted in orderly succession from the apostles and remaining in the Churches to the present day, is to be believed as truth only where it in no way conflicts with ecclesiastical and apostolic tradition". The rule came before the reading and governed the reading.

Third, the living voice of the teacher and the judgment of the bishop. These were two authorities, and they were not the same. The teacher's authority rested on demonstrated wisdom - Gregory learned from Origen not because Origen held an office, but because Origen saw what he could not yet see. The bishop's authority rested on the office handed down - when the villages of the Arsinoite district fell into error, it was Bishop Dionysius who traveled to them and spent three days in open argument, testing their teaching against Scripture. Both were real, and the tension between them was never dissolved.

So no - not Scripture alone. Scripture at the center, bounded by the apostolic rule, and read inside a living community where wisdom and office both carried weight.

No - and we will tell you plainly how the picture you are asking about came to be, and what we actually did.

The catacombs you may be thinking of are Rome's, not ours, and even there they were cemeteries, not hiding places. Christians buried their dead in them, openly and lawfully, for generations. In Alexandria we had no catacombs at all. Our dead were buried in the city's own grounds, the same way everyone else's were.

What we did have were years when meeting openly carried real danger. Under the persecutions - Decius in 250, Valerian in 257, Diocletian in 303 - property was seized, bishops fled, and some believers gave way. During those stretches, yes, assemblies grew quieter or moved. But that was a crisis response, not our regular practice, and it came in waves across two and a half centuries, not as a constant.

Most of our years were not like that. We met in houses, in the open, in the school's hearing room. The Eucharist was celebrated at a table, not in a cave. The school argued with pagan critics by name, in public, in books anyone could read. When Bishop Dionysius went to settle a dispute in the villages, he did it in front of the whole district for three days - no one was hiding.

So here is what is accurate: we had hard years, and in those years people were careful. And here is what is not: the underground church as a constant way of life. That is a later picture, drawn over us. We will not let it stand as though it were ours.

Leadership among us came from three sources, and the balance between them changed across our own years. In the early generations, authority belonged to proven wisdom. The teacher taught because students came - not by appointment, but because the teaching bore fruit in lives. Clement taught, then Origen after him, and their authority was the depth they could open in Scripture and the formation they worked in souls. The second source was the bishop's office. The bishop governed the community's worship, guarded what had been handed down - the rule of faith, the apostolic deposit - and settled disputes. When whole villages in the Arsinoite district fell into a disputed teaching about the end, it was their bishop, Dionysius, who went to them. He sat down for three days of open argument, testing the teaching against Scripture in front of everyone, until he won them back without force. That is our clearest picture of how authority worked well: patient public persuasion, loving the man while honoring the truth more.

The third source arrived late, and it carried power of a different kind. After the council at Nicaea ruled on the confession, the bishop of Alexandria became the enforcer of that agreement across all Egypt, backed by the emperor's hand. Exile became a tool. The same Athanasius who defended Nicaea was driven out five times by emperors who backed the other side. So by the end of our era, authority had three faces: the teacher's wisdom, the bishop's pastoral judgment, and the council's ruling enforced by empire.

The tension between the first two was real and never fully resolved. Origen was ordained without his own bishop's leave, and that bishop, Demetrius, condemned the act and later the man. The church remembered both, rather than erasing either. What stayed constant was this: the apostles' deposit stood fixed, and guarding it was the bishop's charge. Everything else - the open questions Scripture did not settle - was ground where a teacher could walk freely, asking, testing, being wrong, correcting. Formation happened in both channels. The school gave depth to the few who could read and argue. The bishop's governance reached everyone through baptism, the Eucharist, and the Paschal calendar. Neither channel stood alone, and neither swallowed the other - until the emperors entered, and the balance tipped.

When whole villages in the Arsinoite district fell into a disputed teaching about the end, it was their bishop, Dionysius, who went to them.
The third source arrived late, and it carried power of a different kind.
After the council at Nicaea ruled on the confession, the bishop of Alexandria became the enforcer of that agreement across all Egypt, backed by the emperor's hand.
Exile became a tool.
The same Athanasius who defended Nicaea was driven out five times by emperors who backed the other side.
The tension between the first two was real and never fully resolved.
Origen was ordained without his own bishop's leave, and that bishop, Demetrius, condemned the act and later the man.
The church remembered both, rather than erasing either.
Formation happened in both channels.
The bishop's governance reached everyone through baptism, the Eucharist, and the Paschal calendar.
Neither channel stood alone, and neither swallowed the other - until the emperors entered, and the balance tipped.

Our record leaves the wounds visible. Our greatest teacher was driven out, not by pagans, but by his own bishop. The church remembered both men rather than erasing either. Under persecution, many gave way. Some sacrificed to the gods. When peace came, the community fought bitterly over them. The strict party demanded they stay out. The tradition that won here brought the repentant back in, even at the deathbed, and Dionysius defended doing so. After Nicaea, the church itself learned to use exile and condemnation, and some of what was done with that power our own sources report without pride.

At our best, we refused the two easy exits: we did not pretend the failure away, and we did not make the failed unforgivable. Clement told a story he said came from the apostles - John himself traveling to find a young man who had fallen into robbery and violence after his baptism. The old apostle did not write him off. He went after him, on foot, into the mountains, and brought him back. That was the pattern we tried to keep: the soul could turn, even after falling hard, because formation was never finished.

But we also carried the wounds of times when we did worse. The lapsed - those who gave way under threat - tore the community apart. Some bishops were merciful. Others were not. And after the emperors took our side, exile became a tool we used against each other. At our worst, we did what churches with power do.

No present-day church continues our community's exact tradition - that is the honest answer, and we will tell you why.

We were the church of one city and its river country, in the years before the great splits that made today's map. We shared one baptism, one bread and cup, the scriptures, and communion with churches across the whole world. We called ourselves part of the catholic church - the word meant the whole church, the one spread everywhere, as against the sects. It was a claim about wholeness, not the name of a later denomination.

After our years came centuries of division. The council at Chalcedon, in 451, split the Egyptian church from Constantinople and Rome - that fracture runs straight through what we were. Then came the split between East and West. Then the Reformation's many divisions. Every church today that names Alexandria as part of its own past - Coptic Orthodox, Greek Orthodox, Roman Catholic - carries some thread from our world, but none of them carries the whole unbroken cloth, because the cloth itself was torn.

Here is what we can say. We belonged to the one church before those splits. What we held - one God, the Logos made flesh, Scripture as the word that forms souls, baptism and the thanksgiving meal, the rule of faith the apostles handed down - that deposit passed into all the churches that came after. But our particular voice, our way of teaching, our confidence that learning itself is formation, our love of allegory and open inquiry on the unsettled questions - no single present-day church holds all of that exactly as we held it.

We speak from before the map you inherited. We will not tell you which fragment is the true heir, because we are the thing that was whole before the breaking.

The road to baptism - the *photismos*, the enlightening - was long and had stages. We walked it with people, and we did not rush them.

The first step was the turn itself - *pistis*, not agreeing with a list yet, but the soul's first real orientation toward God. A person came because someone brought them, or because they had heard the Scriptures read. They asked to be taught. That asking was the beginning.

Then came the teaching - *katechesis* - and it lasted years, not weeks. They were called catechumens, hearers. They came to the assembly. They heard the Scriptures read and expounded. They learned the prayers. They learned how to live - what to put off, what to take up, how to order a household toward God. In the school, this teaching could go very deep - Gregory tells of years under his teacher, asking questions, testing arguments, until 'like a spark falling on our innermost soul, love was kindled'. For most, it was simpler and shorter, but never instant. The Word himself was working through the teaching - our teachers called him the Instructor, the one who 'cures the unnatural desires of the soul'.

They learned the *kanon* - the rule of faith, the short summary of what the apostles handed down. Father, Son, and Spirit. The Incarnation. The resurrection. The judgment. That rule set the bounds for everything else.

At some point - when the teachers judged they were ready, not when a calendar said so - they were enrolled for baptism. In the final stretch before the water, the teaching intensified. The *mysteria* were opened to them - not puzzles to solve, but depths they would know from inside after they had crossed.

Then came the baptism itself - the *photismos*, the illumination. They went down into the water. They were baptized into the threefold name: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They came up. Athanasius says of the Scriptures, 'These are fountains of salvation, so that anyone who thirsts may be satisfied by the living words they hold' - and the newly baptized drank deeply, because now they could hear the depths. They had crossed.

After the water came the table. They joined the assembly fully now, no longer dismissed before the prayers. The bread, the cup - the *eucharistia*, the thanksgiving - was set before them for the first time as baptized members. And the formation did not stop. Scripture was read to them every week, and the reading itself kept forming them, because the Logos who speaks through it does not run dry. Origen taught that 'just as a human being consists of body, soul, and spirit, so too does Scripture' - there were always more senses to find, always more depth.

That is the shape we can show you. The timing varied - how long someone stayed a hearer depended on their own readiness and the teacher's judgment, not a fixed rule. And we are honest about who this picture represents: it is the urban, Greek-speaking ecology we can document. The villages up the river had the same baptism and the same table, but how the teaching reached them in their own tongue, step by step, our record leaves mostly silent. We will not fill that silence with guesses.

One more thing, because it belongs to honesty. Some who walked this road fell away under persecution - the *lapsi*, those who gave way. When peace came, the church fought bitterly over them. The tradition that won here brought the repentant back, even at the deathbed. The road could be walked twice. That, too, was part of how people joined us - or rejoined us.
